---
title: "Identity modeling"
description: "Three identity schemes and no shared key: probabilistic and deterministic linkage chosen by the evidence, run at stated operating points, and scored against a hidden ground truth."
---

Every finding in this case study rests on one modeling problem: deciding
which records across three systems are the same person. The auction lake
keys leads by UUID, the CRM by an integer id plus a hashed email, and the
marketing exports by an MD5 of the email; no system carries another's key.
The world is built to make that hard in the ways real marketplace data is
hard: people re-apply heavily (a fitted power-law tail, mean 3.8
applications per person, a 100+ tail), identities drift between visits at a
rate that depends on the acquisition channel (about 51% of applications
arrive under a drifted name, email, phone, or zip), about 5% of auction
events lost their CRM record in a simulated migration, timestamps come in
three timezones, and "conversion" means three different things. The
systems and their pathologies are tabulated in the
[appendix](cost.qmd); this page is about the modeling choices and what
they cost.

## Three linkage problems, three tools

The unification is not one matcher. Each link is chosen by the structure
of the evidence, and each runs at a stated operating point that a
downstream analyst can change in one place.

- **Probabilistic where identity is fuzzy.** CRM deduplication and the
  CRM-to-marketing link are [Splink](https://github.com/moj-analytical-services/splink)
  models: term-frequency-adjusted comparisons over name, email, phone, and
  geography, blocked on the fields that survive drift. These are the
  classic record-linkage problems and a Fellegi-Sunter model is the honest
  tool.
- **Deterministic where a model would obscure the truth.** The
  auction-to-CRM linkage is an exact composite key (state, loan amount,
  purpose, FICO band) plus a nine-minute submission window, nearest in
  time. The payload agrees exactly for 100% of true pairs, so the only
  residual errors are payload doppelgangers inside the window, which no
  probabilistic model could separate either. A model would have added
  false confidence, not recall. It also has to absorb a daylight-saving
  fall-back hour where CRM timestamps land 3,600 seconds off.
- **Cluster at the high-precision operating point, not the F1-optimal
  one.** Consumer entities are connected components over dedupe pairs at
  threshold 0.9. At 0.5 the dedupe model is F1-optimal (precision 0.990,
  recall 0.781); at 0.9 precision is 0.9998 and recall 0.764. Transitive
  closure amplifies every false edge into a merged person, so clustering
  trades 1.7 points of recall for a purity of 0.9998 and 98.1% of persons
  kept whole. The link task's F1 barely moves with its threshold (0.879 at
  0.5, 0.877 at 0.99): its ceiling is doppelganger ambiguity, so the
  threshold is not the lever there.
- **A thin spine, wide marts.** Two intermediate models map every lead
  and auction event to its resolved consumer entity; wide denormalized
  marts join through that spine so no dashboard query joins more than one
  table.

## The scorecard

Scored against the hidden crosswalk
([er/scorecard.json](https://github.com/JordanBeary/tributary/blob/main/er/scorecard.json)):

| Task | Precision | Recall | F1 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CRM to marketing link (probabilistic, best match per lead) | 0.895 | 0.864 | **0.879** |
| CRM dedupe (probabilistic, pairwise, threshold 0.5) | 0.990 | 0.781 | **0.873** |
| CRM dedupe at the clustering operating point (threshold 0.9) | 0.9998 | 0.764 | 0.866 |
| Auction to CRM linkage (deterministic) | 0.995 (lead) | 0.998 (non-orphan) | — |

Downstream identity quality: weighted cluster purity 0.9998, 98.1% of
persons unsplit, and **635,579 resolved consumers**^[The scorecard reports
636,164 clusters because it clusters every CRM lead; 635,579 is the count
of resolved consumers with at least one auctioned lead (`dim_consumer`),
which is the population every finding and model on this site is computed
over. The site uses 635,579 throughout.] against 2.40M auction lead ids and
2.28M CRM rows.

**The headline:** 95.3% of auction events are consumer-joinable after
unification, against a >95% target and 0% before. Of the 4.7% gap, almost
all is the ~5% migration-orphan population that is unjoinable by
construction; the linkage recovers 99.8% of what is recoverable.

## Why these numbers can be trusted

The simulator generates every consumer with a true `consumer_key`, strips
it from all three silos, and keeps it in a private crosswalk that never
enters the cloud. The linkage works blind, exactly as a real team would,
and is then scored against the crosswalk. Every number above is a
measurement, not an assertion.

Difficulty was engineered, not assumed. The first fracture scored link F1
0.976 and dedupe F1 0.997, both at the ceiling their own ambiguity allowed;
a synthetic benchmark you can ace is not a benchmark. The repeat-application
distribution and the channel-dependent drift were supplied from industry
experience, the target band was moved to 0.8-0.9, and the first run under
the new engine landed both tasks in band with no dial iteration.

::: {.callout-note title="How this number was decided"}
The first entity-resolution run scored link F1 0.976 and dedupe F1 0.997 — above the design's own band — and the agent flagged its result as too clean rather than reporting it (decision D8). It recommended turning the pathology dials up; the human did, but not the way the agent proposed: the author supplied a one-year leads-per-contact distribution from industry experience and a channel-dependent identity-drift mechanism, and moved the target band down to 0.8–0.9 (prompt P-010; the raw table never entered the repository, its fitted form did). The next full run landed at 0.879 and 0.873 on the default dials, which is why the scorecard above is evidence and not a benchmark the simulator was built to pass. Records: D8, P-010, C18 in the [decision and prompt logs](https://github.com/JordanBeary/tributary/tree/main/meta/logs); the chain is drawn on the [method page](method.qmd).
:::

## What identity error does to a decision

Every downstream number inherits the linkage's error, so the case study
measures the propagation once rather than assuming it away: the
[nurture experiment](dashboards.qmd#the-nurture-experiment-and-who-to-message)
compares the per-segment lift recovered through the F1-0.88 link against
the effect the simulator injected. Linkage noise attenuates the recovered
effect; it does not fabricate one. That is the property a decision-maker
needs from an identity layer.

## What the unified identity paid for

- The 3.8x consumer overcount and the **$12.0M (5.7% of revenue)** buyers
  paid for consumers they had already bought within 30 days: the
  [identity and duplicate-spend finding](dashboards.qmd).
- Channel ROAS from 0.94x to 3.06x, computable only once revenue joins
  through the auction: the [attribution finding](dashboards.qmd).
- Consumer-entity history (application sequence, recency, prior sales) as
  the strongest features in the [models](models.qmd), and the recency
  buckets the [strategy memo](strategy-memo.qmd) prices reserves against.
